Summarize a Fitted Model

Source: R/inference.R
summary.StatmodFit.Rd

Returns one coefficient table per distribution parameter, carrying the estimate, its standard error, the statistic of the test named by test (Wald's by default), its p-value and an interval, together with the degrees of freedom, the information criteria and the notes that qualify the numbers.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
summary(
  object,
  level = 0.95,
  vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(),
  correct = FALSE,
  test = wald_test(),
  max_coef = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

level

The confidence level.

vcov_type

A vcov_method object, the variance matrix, passed to vcov.StatmodFit(): bayesian_vcov() (the default), frequentist_vcov() or unconditional_vcov(). The information from which the standard errors are computed is an argument of each of them (distributions7::observed_info() by default). The last carries the uncertainty of the hyperparameters into every standard error under it, where correct carries the same uncertainty into the degrees of freedom; the two are the same quantity read on two surfaces, and both can be used in one call. The conventions are compared at vcov_method. The effective degrees of freedom of the summary are read on this same information (see the section on the degrees of freedom).

correct

Whether the degrees of freedom include the cost of estimating the hyperparameters. The ordinary count treats them as known although they were estimated from the same data, so a criterion built on it is too generous. See statmod_edf_correction(). The default is FALSE, which leaves the count unchanged; the correction is zero where no hyperparameter was estimated by a marginal criterion.

test

A test_statistic object, the statistic that the coefficient tables report. wald_test() (the default) reads the variance matrix and refits nothing. lr_test(), score_test() and gradient_test() cost one restricted refit per row and are reported as a signed root. The four are compared at test_statistic; see also statmod_stat_at(). A character string is rejected with an error.

max_coef

How many coefficient rows each block of the printed summary shows, Inf or NA for all of them. NULL, the default, reads the option statmodels7.summary_max_coef, and 10 where that is unset. A hyperparameter row is never hidden, whatever this is, and a block of twelve rows or fewer is never abridged. The value is carried on the result, so summary(fit, max_coef = Inf) prints in full at the console; print.StatmodSummary() takes the same argument for an object already in hand.

...

Passed to vcov.StatmodFit().

Value

A StatmodSummary().

Details

Each distribution parameter is read as blocks, not as one list of coefficients, because most coefficients of a fitted model are not quantities of interest in themselves. The blocks are

the parametric terms

every unpenalized term together, one row per coefficient, which is the ordinary table.

one block per smooth

the linear component's coefficient where the construction carries one, the smoothing parameter, and the effective degrees of freedom. The coefficients of the wiggly part are not shown: they are coordinates in an orthonormal basis, a single one of them has no interpretation, and together they determine the edf.

one block per random effect

the parameters of the distribution of the effects, usually called the variance components, the edf and a summary of the predicted effects. The effects themselves, of which there is one per level, are not listed.

one block per selection

a lasso, a SCAD or an MCP: its hyperparameters, how many coefficients survived, and those coefficients. The ones set exactly to zero are counted, not listed.

one block per other penalized term

its coefficients, which stay interpretable under a ridge, together with its hyperparameters.

one block per break-point term

the quantities that the term reports (slopes, changes and positions), with standard errors from the delta method applied to the coefficients through which the term is fitted. A position carries no test.

one block per structural term

the term's own parameters (a filter's level, loadings and persistences, or the transition probabilities of a regime chain), with a level that an intercept holds marked as held.

The effective degrees of freedom

The edf of a term is its share of \(\mathrm{tr}[(H+S)^{-1}H]\), with \(H\) the information of the log-likelihood and \(S\) the second derivative of the penalty, read over the coefficients of every equation at once. The summary reads \(H\) on the information of vcov_type (distributions7::default_information() of the family where the information of the variance object is NULL), which is the matrix that the standard errors above the edf invert. A call with vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(information = expected_info()) therefore prints the standard errors and the edf on the expected information. The count stored in fit@edf was read at fit time on the information of the outer criterion: the observed information by default under reml() and ml(). With the defaults the two coincide, and the summary recomputes the count only where vcov_type names the other matrix.

Three cases keep the count stored in the fit. Under aic() and bic() the count is part of the criterion that prices the fit, and it is read on the information of that criterion, so the summary leaves it as it is and the printed criterion stays reproducible from it. A model with a structural term is read on the joint vector of the coefficients and the term's own parameters, as before. A variance object without an information property has no matrix to read.

The eigenvalues of \((H+S)^{-1}H\) are \(v^\top H v/(v^\top H v + v^\top S v)\), for the generalized eigenvectors \(v\). They lie in \([0, 1]\), and the total in \([0, p]\) with \(p\) the number of coefficients, when \(H\) is positive semidefinite. The observed information can be indefinite (a Student t at an outlier, for example). A direction with \(v^\top H v < 0\) then contributes a negative share, an edf can be underestimated, and the bounds above can fail. The summary adds a note when the observed information used for the count has an eigenvalue below \(-p\,\epsilon\,\lambda_{\max}\) (\(\epsilon\) the machine epsilon and \(\lambda_{\max}\) the largest eigenvalue), the floor with which the package separates a flat direction from rounding. The expected information is positive semidefinite and carries no such note.

A hyperparameter is the first row of its block, since it governs every coefficient under it, and its name carries a mark in square brackets that gives the source of the value. A hyperparameter estimated by reml() or ml() maximizes a twice differentiable criterion, so it carries a standard error and an interval, both read on the free scale that its link defines and mapped back (statmod_hyper_vcov()). One chosen by aic(), bic() or cv() along a path over a kinked penalty is the argument of a minimum over a grid, so the row names the criterion and leaves the remaining columns empty: there is no curvature at such a point from which to read a standard error. A smooth penalty under aic() or bic() is minimized over its free scale, and its row also has no standard error, because the criterion is not a likelihood. A hyperparameter that the term holds is marked fixed, and one that stayed at the starting value of its term because the outer criterion was not run is marked start.

The statistic column reports the test named by test. By default it is Wald's, the estimate over its standard error, which is the only one of the four that needs no refit and is read only from the unrestricted fit. The other three – the likelihood ratio, Rao's score and Terrell's gradient – hold the coefficient at the null value and refit, one refit per row, and are reported as the signed root of their \(\chi^2_1\) statistic with the sign of \(\hat\beta_j - b\), so that the column carries one kind of quantity whichever test was requested and Wald's own \(z\) is the case where that root is exact. The p-value is the \(\chi^2_1\) one in every case, and for Wald the two readings agree identically.

Only the statistic and its p-value change with test: the interval stays the Wald one, since inverting a test requires many refits for each coefficient. confint.StatmodFit() inverts the same test through its test argument, one coefficient at a time. A row for which the restricted fit is not defined – a coefficient under a kinked penalty, an aliased one, any coefficient of a model carrying a structural term – reports NA instead of the Wald value, so the column never carries two tests at once. Every other row is tested, including a smooth's own coordinates and a random effect's, on the penalized objective and with the reading described in statmod_stat_at(). A quantity of a break-point term that is one coefficient carries the restricted statistic of that coefficient; a quantity that combines several coefficients, and the position of a break-point, carry none.

The meaning of a Wald p-value depends on the row. For an unpenalized coefficient it is the ordinary p-value. For a coefficient in a penalized block it is conditional on the smoothing parameter, which was not estimated jointly with it, and it does not account for the shrinkage of the estimate toward zero. For a coefficient that a kinked penalty selected, the row exists only because that coefficient survived the selection, and a naive interval there under-covers.

The degrees of freedom are the effective ones, summed over the terms, so a penalized term counts the degrees of freedom that it uses instead of the number of its columns. The information criteria are built on that count: aic is \(-2\ell + 2\,\mathrm{df}\) and bic replaces the factor 2 by the logarithm of the sum of the prior weights, which are frequency weights.

Reading the foot

Below the criteria the summary describes the point at which the fit stopped with a few numbers from statmod_certificate(). The summary prints no verdict. Each number is dimensionless, so it does not change with the units of a coefficient.

inner max |grad|/se

the largest \(|g_j|/\sqrt{A_{jj}}\) over the coefficients, where \(g\) is the gradient of the penalized objective and \(A\) its curvature, the penalized information. \(1/\sqrt{A_{jj}}\) is the standard error of coefficient \(j\) conditional on the others, which is smaller than the marginal one that the tables print, and the ratio equals \(\sqrt{2\Delta_j}\) with \(\Delta_j = g_j^2/(2A_{jj})\) the gain in log-likelihood of a Newton step in that coordinate alone. At a mode it is small. For a model carrying a score-driven filter it covers the filter's own parameters as well. It leaves out a coefficient that a kinked penalty has set to zero, a frozen working block, and an aliased column, and it is read on the directions that the kinks of a break-point sitting on an observation leave free.

inner min eigen

the smallest eigenvalue of \(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\) with \(D = \mathrm{diag}(A)\), the curvature rescaled to a unit diagonal. It is at most one. Near one the coordinates are well separated; near zero some combination of them is barely identified, as two nearly collinear covariates or an intercept beside a random effect make it; below zero the point is not a mode.

zeros max |score|/kink

printed only where a kinked penalty (a lasso, an elastic net, a SCAD or an MCP) set coefficients exactly to zero, together with how many. At a zero the penalty has no derivative and the coefficient no standard error, so the condition for an optimum is \(|s_j| \le \kappa_j\): the derivative of the log-likelihood in that coefficient within the size of the kink, \(\lambda\) for a lasso. The number is the largest \(|s_j|/\kappa_j\). At or below one every zero is an optimum; above one a coefficient would improve the objective by leaving zero. A reading \(r\) below one means that the coefficient with the largest ratio is held by the kink with a margin of \(1 - r\); if the other coefficients were fixed it would leave zero at a \(\lambda\) smaller by the factor \(r\). Along a path the others move too, and the threshold moves with them. The number is not a test of significance, only a check on whether the zeros agree with the \(\lambda\) of the fit, and values close to one are ordinary where \(\lambda\) was chosen on a grid, because the next coefficient to enter is close to its threshold by construction.

outer max |grad|/se and min eigen

the same two readings for the criterion that estimated the hyperparameters, on the free scale that their links define, printed only where reml() or ml() ran. The curvature is the negated Hessian of the criterion. A hyperparameter that ran to the edge of its chart is left out, because its curvature collapses with its gradient; where every one did the line reads not available: at a boundary. A hyperparameter chosen along a path has no gradient, and there is no outer line.

See also

vcov.StatmodFit(), confint.StatmodFit(), test_statistic, vcov_method, statmod_test(), which computes the same four statistics for one coefficient against a value that need not be zero, and statmod_stat_at()

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(120))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(120, sd = 0.4)
summary(statmod(y ~ x | sigma ~ x,
                distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd))
#> A statmod fit
#> 
#> Call:  statmod(formula = y ~ x | sigma ~ x, distrib = distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), 
#>             data = dd)

#>   x               1.903  0.1313 14.49 < 1e-16  1.645  2.16
#> 
#> === sigma   [log link]
#> 
#> Parametric terms
#>                estimate     se       z         p   lower   upper
#>   (Intercept)   -0.9559 0.1338  -7.144 9.051e-13  -1.218 -0.6936
#>   x             0.02082 0.2277 0.09145    0.9271 -0.4254   0.467
#> 
#> 95% intervals, bayesian variance
#> conditional log-likelihood -55.852571    effective df 4.00
